h1: Making a spiced rum: building the recipe and the brand together
title: Making a Spiced Rum: Recipe and Brand | Craft Beer School
desc: How to build a spiced rum: choosing the base rum, spices, sugar and maceration, then shaping a brand around what is in the bottle.
teaser: Vanilla, cinnamon and orange peel are easy to buy. A spiced rum that tastes the same every batch is not.
standfirst: Spiced rum lets a small producer create a distinctive product without decades of ageing. The recipe and the brand should be designed together, because what you promise on the label has to be in the glass every time. Here is how to build both.
sections:
A spiced rum is rum flavoured with spices and other botanicals, often sweetened and coloured. The base sets the ceiling for quality. A clean, light rum lets the spices lead. A heavier, more aromatic rum brings its own molasses, fruit and funk that the spices must work with.

Most Indian rum is made from molasses, the by-product of sugar refining. Our guide to molasses and grain spirit in India covers how that base is made. Taste several base rums at the same strength before you design anything. If the base has harsh or solvent notes, spices will not hide them for long.

Most spiced rums build on a familiar core:

  • Vanilla for sweetness and roundness.
  • Cinnamon or cassia for warmth.
  • Clove, nutmeg and allspice for depth. Use them carefully, because clove in particular takes over fast.
  • Orange or other citrus peel for lift.
  • Ginger and black pepper for heat.

India gives you a strong local palette: Kerala pepper, nutmeg and mace, cardamom from the Western Ghats, jaggery, kokum and local citrus. These can give a spiced rum a clear identity. Check that every ingredient is permitted for use in spirits. Keep records of supplier and lot.

The simplest method is maceration: steep the spices in the rum at a fixed strength for a fixed time, then filter them out. Higher alcohol extracts flavour faster and pulls out more oils. Longer steeps pull more tannin and bitterness, especially from woody spices.

Start by macerating each spice on its own in small jars, at the same strength and for the same number of days. Taste every few days. That gives you a library of single spice extracts to blend on the bench. It is the same discipline gin makers use with botanicals.

Once you have a blend you like, macerate the full recipe together and taste it daily until it hits the target, then filter. Some producers distil part of the spice mix or use prepared extracts to get more consistency.

Many spiced rums are sweetened. Sugar changes the drink a lot. It rounds off the alcohol and lifts vanilla and spice, but too much makes the rum cloying. Add sugar in measured steps, record grams per litre and test it neat, with ice and with a mixer.

Colour usually comes from caramel and from the spices themselves. Rules on minimum bottling strength, permitted additives and what can be called rum vary by country and by Indian state. Check the current standards before you fix your recipe or label. Bottling strength also changes how the spices taste, so decide it before final blending.

Spices vary by harvest and storage. One lot of vanilla or cinnamon can be noticeably stronger than the last. Write a specification for each spice, taste each new lot against the last and adjust the dose to hit your reference. Keep a retained sample of every batch.

Train a small tasting panel to compare each batch against the reference in the same glasses and at the same strength. This is where many small producers struggle. A spiced rum that changes every batch loses drinkers who liked the first bottle.
Designing the brand with the recipe

The recipe and the brand should tell the same story. If the label promises Kerala spices, the rum should taste of them. If the brand is about a rich, dessert-like sip, the sugar and vanilla must deliver that. If it is built for highballs, test it with soda, cola and ginger ale and design the flavour to cut through.

Work out positioning early. Who drinks it, when and against which rums on the shelf? Our guide to beer brand positioning sets out a method that works for spirits too. Then let that answer decide the spices, sweetness and strength.

Taste it the way your customer will. In much of India that means with ice, in heat, often with a mixer, sometimes with food. Responsible serving suggestions on the label and in your marketing belong in the brand from the start.
faqs: What spices go into spiced rum?
Most use vanilla, cinnamon or cassia, clove, nutmeg, allspice and citrus peel. Indian producers often add pepper, cardamom or other local spices.
How long should spices macerate in rum?
It depends on strength and spice. Test single spices first, then macerate the blend and taste daily until it hits your reference.
Is sugar allowed in spiced rum?
Sweetening is common, but rules on additives and naming vary by country and Indian state. Check the current standard before finalising.
How do I keep spiced rum consistent?
Write a specification for each spice, taste every new lot against the last and compare each batch with a retained reference sample.
